items.prompt: What is the approximate speed of light in a vacuum?
rubric: Light travels at about 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum.
The other values confuse it with much slower speeds such as that of sound.

items.prompt: Which statement is one of the two postulates of special relativity?

options.label: Time passes at the same rate for all observers
Mass and energy are always conserved separately
The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames
The speed of light depends on the speed of its source

rubric: The first postulate says the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame.
Distractors state classical assumptions that relativity rejects.

items.prompt: Which equation expresses the rest energy of an object of mass m?

options.label: E = m^2 c
E = mc^2
E = mc

rubric: Einstein's relation is E = mc^2.
E = (1/2) mc^2 is a confusion with classical kinetic energy.

items.prompt: Which expression gives the Lorentz factor gamma for speed v?

options.label: sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)

rubric: Gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), which is at least 1.
Other options drop the square root, flip the fraction or change the sign.

items.prompt: Who published the special theory of relativity in 1905?

options.label: Isaac Newton
Albert Einstein
Max Planck
Niels Bohr

rubric: Einstein published it in 1905.
The others are famous physicists but not the author of the theory.

items.prompt: Which of the following are inertial frames of reference? Select all that apply.

options.label: A car moving at constant velocity on a straight, level road
A spaceship coasting with engines off, far from any large mass
A car driving around a sharp bend at constant speed
A rocket accelerating upward during launch

rubric: An inertial frame moves at constant velocity without acceleration.
Turning or speeding up means acceleration, so those frames are not inertial.

items.prompt: A student measures the length of a metal rod lying at rest on a lab bench. The problem sheet says this is a special kind of length measurement used in relativity formulas. What is the name of the length measured in the frame where the object is at rest?

options.label: Relativistic length
Apparent length
Proper length
Contracted length

rubric: Proper length is the length measured in the object's own rest frame.
Contracted length is what other frames in relative motion measure.

items.prompt: A spaceship passes Earth at 0.8c. According to observers on Earth, how does the ship's clock compare with their own clocks?

options.label: It runs faster than theirs
It stops completely
It runs slower than theirs
It runs at the same rate

rubric: A moving clock runs slow in the observer's frame, by a factor gamma.
Faster or identical rates ignore dilation, and the clock does not stop unless v = c.

items.prompt: A long spaceship flies past you at 0.9c. Which of its dimensions do you measure as contracted?

options.label: Only the height, perpendicular to motion
None, the contraction is an optical illusion
Only the length along the direction of motion
All dimensions by the same fraction

rubric: Length contraction acts only along the direction of relative motion.
Distractors apply it to the wrong dimensions or deny that it is real.

items.prompt: Two lightning bolts strike at the same instant in the ground frame, at the front and back of a passing train. What does a train passenger generally find?

options.label: The strikes are simultaneous, since events are absolute
Both strikes happen at the same place in the train frame
The passenger sees no strikes because of contraction
The strikes are generally not simultaneous for the passenger

rubric: Simultaneity depends on the frame, so events at different places can differ in timing.
Distractors assume time is absolute, as in classical mechanics.

items.prompt: Why can an object with mass not be accelerated all the way to the speed of light?

options.label: Gamma falls toward zero, so its energy vanishes at c
Light pushes back on it with growing force at high speed
Its mass shrinks to zero as its speed approaches c
Its energy grows without limit as its speed approaches c

rubric: Energy equals gamma times mc^2, and gamma diverges as v approaches c.
Distractors misstate how mass or gamma behave near c.

items.prompt: What does E = mc^2 tell us about a small mass at rest?

options.label: It has the same energy as any object, whatever its mass
It has a huge energy content, because c^2 is very large
It can only hold energy when it is near the speed of light
It has no energy until it starts moving at high speed

rubric: Mass is a form of energy, and c^2 makes the equivalent energy enormous.
Distractors claim energy exists only with motion or is independent of mass.

items.prompt: Two spaceships pass each other at 0.6c. Which statements are consistent with special relativity? Select all that apply.

options.label: Both observers measure the same speed of light
One observer can prove that they are truly at rest
Both observers agree on every time interval measured
Each observer finds the other's clock running slow

rubric: Light speed is invariant, and time dilation is symmetric between inertial observers.
There is no absolute rest frame, and time intervals differ between frames.

items.prompt: Muons are made high in the atmosphere and live about 2.2 microseconds at rest. Even at nearly c, classical physics predicts they would travel only about 660 m, yet many reach the ground several km below. What best explains this?

options.label: Muons speed up beyond c as they fall toward Earth
Earth's frame sees the muons' clocks run slow, so they live longer
The muons decay on time, but the atmosphere is thinner
Gravity stretches the muon lifetime as they descend

rubric: Time dilation lengthens the lifetime measured in Earth's frame, allowing a longer path.
Distractors invoke faster-than-light motion, gravity or atmosphere rather than dilation.

items.prompt: Which statement is one of the two postulates of Einstein's special relativity?

options.label: A moving emitter adds its own speed to the speed of the light it sends
Light travels at c only relative to the source that emitted it
The speed of light in vacuum is the same for all inertial observers
Light moves through a medium, so its speed depends on the observer

rubric: The constancy of c in all inertial frames is the second postulate.
Distractors reflect ether or Galilean velocity-addition thinking.

items.prompt: A spaceship passes Earth at 0.8c. How do Earth observers say the ship's clock runs compared with their own clocks?

options.label: Faster than theirs, because the ship's motion speeds up its ticks
The same as theirs, because all inertial frames share one time
Slower only in appearance, because signals from the ship are delayed
Slower than theirs, because moving clocks tick at a reduced rate

rubric: Time dilation: a clock moving relative to the observer is measured to run slow.
The last distractor confuses real dilation with a light-travel-time effect.

items.prompt: In special relativity, what is meant by the proper time between two events?

options.label: Time between the events measured in the laboratory frame only
Time between the events measured by the observer who sees them first
The longest time between the events found by any inertial observer
Time between the events measured by a clock present at both events

rubric: Proper time is measured by one clock at both events and is the shortest interval.
Distractors treat it as the longest or as tied to a special observer.

items.prompt: A metre stick moves very fast relative to you. Along which direction is its length contracted in your measurement?

options.label: In no direction; it is only an optical illusion from light delay
Equally in all directions around the stick
Only along the direction of relative motion
Only perpendicular to the direction of relative motion

rubric: Length contraction occurs only parallel to the relative motion.
Distractors misplace the direction or deny the effect is real.

items.prompt: Two lightning bolts hit the two ends of a train at the same moment in the ground frame. A passenger at the centre of the train is moving toward the front. In the passenger's frame, which statement holds?

options.label: Which came first depends on the passenger's seat
The rear strike occurred before the front strike
The two strikes still occurred at the same moment
The front strike occurred before the rear strike

rubric: Relativity of simultaneity: the strike in the direction of motion happens first for the moving observer.
Distractors assume absolute simultaneity or reverse the order.

items.prompt: Which quantities have the same value for all inertial observers in special relativity? Select all that apply.

options.label: The speed of light in vacuum
The time between two events as measured in each frame
The rest mass of a particle
The proper time between two events
The length of a rod moving past the observer

rubric: c, proper time and rest mass are invariant.
Moving lengths and frame-measured time intervals depend on the observer.

items.prompt: Cosmic-ray muons form about 15 km above the ground and move at about 0.99c. Their rest lifetime is 2.2 microseconds, enough to travel only about 660 m without relativity. Yet many reach the ground. From the ground frame, what best explains this?

options.label: Their rest lifetime is longer in the atmosphere than in a lab
Their speed exceeds c in air, so they outrun their decay
Earth's gravity slows their clocks enough to extend the lifetime
Their moving clocks run slow, so their lifetime in the ground frame is much longer

rubric: Time dilation lengthens the muon's lifetime as measured on the ground.
Distractors invoke faster-than-light motion, changed rest lifetime, or gravity.

items.prompt: A spaceship moves past Earth at 0.6c. A clock on the ship records 10 s between two events at the ship. How long between the events does Earth measure?

options.label: 8 s

rubric: 8 s multiplies by 1/gamma; 16.7 s divides by beta instead.

items.prompt: A rod has a proper length of 10 m. It moves at 0.8c along its length past an observer. What length does the observer measure?

options.label: 8 m
6 m

rubric: gamma = 5/3, so L = 10/gamma = 6 m.
8 m uses beta directly; 16.7 m multiplies by gamma.

items.prompt: What is the rest energy of 1 gram of matter? Use c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.
rubric: Other options forget the gram-to-kilogram conversion or use the classical 1/2 factor.

items.prompt: A ship moves at 0.6c relative to Earth and fires a projectile forward at 0.6c relative to the ship. What is the projectile's speed relative to Earth?
rubric: 1.2c is simple Galilean addition, which fails near c.

items.prompt: Frame S' moves at 0.6c along +x relative to S. An event has x = 8 light-minutes and t = 5 minutes in S. Using x' = gamma(x - vt), what is x'?

options.label: 4 light-minutes
5 light-minutes
10 light-minutes
6.25 light-minutes

rubric: vt = 3 light-minutes, so x' = 1.25 x (8 - 3) = 6.25 light-minutes.
5 is the Galilean result; 10 omits vt; 4 multiplies by 0.8.

items.prompt: A probe passes Earth at 0.6c. A clock on the probe records 20 s between two events that both occur at the probe. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: The Lorentz factor for the probe is 1.25
Earth's measured interval is the proper time
The 20 s is the proper time between the events
Earth observers measure 25 s between the events
Earth observers measure 16 s between the events

rubric: gamma = 1.25, so Earth measures 25 s while 20 s is the proper time.
16 s wrongly contracts the time; the Earth interval is not proper time.

items.prompt: A star is 4 light-years from Earth in Earth's frame. A spacecraft travels there at 0.8c. Earth observers calculate the trip takes 5 years. How long does the trip take on the spacecraft's own clock?

options.label: 3 years
5 years
4 years
6.25 years

rubric: Proper time = 5 yr / gamma = 5 x 0.6 = 3 years.
5 is Earth's time; 6.25 multiplies by gamma; 4 ignores speed.

items.prompt: A muon has a proper lifetime of 2.2 microseconds and moves at 0.8c relative to the lab (gamma = 5/3). Roughly how far does it travel in the lab before decaying? Use c = 3.0e8 m/s.

options.label: About 1470 m
About 1100 m
About 880 m
About 530 m

rubric: Lab lifetime is (5/3)(2.2 us) = 3.67 us, and 0.8c times that is about 880 m.
530 m forgets time dilation; 1470 m applies gamma twice.

items.prompt: A spaceship of proper length 120 m moves at 0.8c past a marker fixed in a station's frame. How long does the station's clock record for the ship to pass the marker? Use c = 3.0e8 m/s.
rubric: The station sees the ship contracted to 72 m, so t = 72 m / (2.4e8 m/s) = 3.0e-7 s.
5.0e-7 s ignores contraction; 8.3e-7 s wrongly lengthens the ship.

items.prompt: Relative to Earth, a probe moves at 0.6c. It fires a pulse forward at 0.6c relative to the probe. What is the pulse's speed relative to Earth?
rubric: 1.20c is the classical sum, which breaks the speed limit.

items.prompt: A particle of mass m moves at 0.6c relative to the lab (gamma = 1.25). What is its kinetic energy in the lab?
rubric: Relativistic KE = (gamma - 1)mc^2 = 0.25 mc^2.
0.18 mc^2 is the classical (1/2)mv^2; 1.25 mc^2 is the total energy, not the kinetic part.

items.prompt: In frame S an event occurs at x = 300 m and t = 1.0 microsecond. Frame S' moves at +0.6c along x relative to S, with origins coinciding at t = 0 (gamma = 1.25, c = 3.0e8 m/s). What is the event's x' coordinate in S'?
rubric: 600 m uses the wrong sign; 120 m forgets gamma.

items.prompt: A clock moves at 0.6c relative to the lab (gamma = 1.25). Which statements about lab measurements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: A 5 m rod at rest in the clock's frame, lying along the motion, measures 4 m in the lab.
A 5 m rod at rest in the clock's frame, perpendicular to the motion, measures 4 m in the lab.
10 s of proper time on the clock corresponds to 12.5 s on lab clocks.
A particle of mass m at rest in the clock's frame has lab total energy 1.25 mc^2.
10 s of proper time on the clock corresponds to 8 s on lab clocks.

rubric: Dilation multiplies by gamma, contraction along motion divides by gamma, and total energy is gamma mc^2.
Lengths perpendicular to the motion do not contract, and dividing time by gamma is the reversed direction.

items.prompt: A probe leaves Earth for a star that is 8 light-years away in Earth's frame. It travels at a steady 0.8c, so Earth observers expect it to arrive after 10 years. Mission planners want to know how much the probe's own clock will advance during this one-way trip. What is it?

options.label: 12.5 years
6 years
10 years
8 years

rubric: Proper time = 10 yr / gamma = 10 / (5/3) = 6 years.
12.5 years multiplies by gamma instead of dividing; 10 years ignores dilation.

items.prompt: Two lightning bolts strike the two ends of a train simultaneously in the ground frame. A passenger at the train's midpoint, moving toward the front, receives both flashes. What does the passenger conclude about the emission events?

options.label: Both struck together, since light travels at the same speed toward both ends.
Both struck together, since the passenger sits at the exact midpoint of the train.
The front bolt struck first, since in the train frame the events are not simultaneous.
The rear bolt struck first, since the passenger is moving away from that flash.

rubric: The passenger meets the front flash first, and with equal distances and equal light speed, infers the front strike came first.
The 'together' options ignore that simultaneity is frame-dependent.

items.prompt: A student estimates a muon's chance of reaching the ground by using the dilated lab lifetime (about 15 microseconds) and also the contracted atmosphere thickness (about 1.4 km) in the same calculation. What is wrong with this?

options.label: The two effects cancel exactly, so the survival ratio must match the non-relativistic result anyway.
Contraction applies only to solid objects, never to distances such as an atmosphere, so that value is invalid.
Dilation applies only in the muon's frame, so the lab lifetime must be shorter than 2.2 microseconds.
Dilation and contraction describe the same trip from different frames, so using both counts gamma twice.

rubric: Use lab time with lab distance, or muon time with contracted distance, never a mix.
Distractors misassign where each effect applies or claim a false cancellation.

items.prompt: In frame S, event P is at x = 0, t = 0 and event Q is at x = 3 light-seconds, t = 5 s. Which statement is correct?

options.label: Every frame measures exactly 5 s between P and Q, since time is shared.
Some frame sees P and Q at the same place, 4 s apart on its clock.
No frame can see them at one place, since they are 3 light-seconds apart.
Some frame sees P and Q simultaneous, 3 light-seconds apart in space.

rubric: The interval is timelike: sqrt(25 - 9) = 4 s of proper time in a frame where both occur at one place.
Simultaneity is impossible for timelike separation, and time intervals differ between frames.

items.prompt: A 20 m (proper length) ladder moves at 0.866c (gamma = 2) toward a barn of proper length 10 m. In the barn frame, both doors are shut at the same instant with the ladder inside. In the ladder frame the barn is only 5 m long. Why is there no contradiction?

options.label: The doors close at different times in the ladder frame, so the ladder is never fully enclosed there.
The ladder is physically compressed to 5 m, so it fits in both frames at once.
Contraction does not apply to rigid objects, so the ladder never actually fits.
Only the barn frame is valid, since the barn is the object truly at rest.

rubric: Simultaneity of the door closings is frame-dependent, which resolves the paradox.
Distractors assume a single absolute answer or deny contraction.

items.prompt: Twin A stays on Earth while twin B travels to a star and back at constant speed on each leg. During the legs, each twin sees the other's clock run slow. Why does B end up younger rather than the result being symmetric?

options.label: Signals from B arrive late, so B's actual age equals A's despite appearances.
B's turnaround switches inertial frames, so the two histories are not symmetric.
B's clock is slowed by acceleration itself, so dilation exists only at the turnaround.
Earth is the only true rest frame, so A's clock gives the real elapsed time.

rubric: Only B changes inertial frames, so B's path through spacetime has less proper time.
Acceleration is not the cause of the age gap, and the result is not a signal-delay illusion.

items.prompt: Two observers in uniform relative motion compare measurements of the same events. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: The time between two events at one place in a frame is the longest value any frame measures.
Length contraction is only an optical illusion from light-travel delays, so no ruler truly shortens.
Both observers measure the same speed for a given light pulse.
Two events with spacelike separation can occur in opposite orders in different frames.
Each observer finds the other's clock runs slow when using their own synchronised clocks.

rubric: Reciprocal dilation, order reversal for spacelike events and invariant c are all standard results.
Proper time is the shortest interval, and contraction is a genuine measured effect, not a visual illusion.

items.prompt: Earth observers see ships A and B approaching each other along a line, each at 0.9c relative to Earth. A student adds the speeds to get 1.8c for B as seen from A and claims relativity is violated. What is B's speed in A's frame, and what flaw does the student's reasoning have?

options.label: About 0.90c, because invariance of light speed fixes every relative speed measurement.
About 0.45c, because each ship's speed must be divided by gamma before adding them.
About 0.994c, because velocities combine with a denominator 1 + v1v2/c^2 rather than adding simply.
About 1.8c, because only signals and masses are capped at c, not relative speeds.

rubric: u = 1.8c / (1 + 0.81) = 0.994c, since the Galilean sum is invalid near c.
1.8c is only the closing speed in Earth's frame, not B's speed in A's frame.

items.prompt: Muons created high in the atmosphere at 0.98c reach the ground in far greater numbers than a classical estimate predicts. Which analysis in the muon's own rest frame is consistent with the Earth-frame explanation of time dilation?

options.label: The atmosphere keeps its thickness but the muon's clock runs fast, so decay happens after it reaches the ground
The muon's lifetime is stretched, so it survives longer than its proper lifetime in its own frame before it decays
Both the muon lifetime and the atmosphere thickness stay fixed, and only the Earth observer sees any effect
The atmosphere is length-contracted, so the muon covers a shorter distance within its short proper lifetime

rubric: In the muon frame its lifetime is the proper lifetime, and the atmosphere moves past it and is contracted.
Distractors wrongly apply dilation in the muon's own frame or deny frame-dependent lengths.

items.prompt: Two lightning bolts strike opposite ends of a platform simultaneously in the platform frame. A train moves along the platform in the +x direction. Which statement about the train's frame is correct?

options.label: The front strike (larger x) occurs first, since t' = γ(t − vx/c^2) is smaller for larger x
The rear strike occurs first, since the train moves away from it and its light needs more time to catch up
The strikes stay simultaneous, since both have the same t and the train's speed only changes lengths
The order depends on where the train's midpoint was, not on its direction, so no general ordering exists

rubric: The Lorentz time transformation gives a smaller t' for the event at larger x when v is positive.
Distractors treat simultaneity as absolute or confuse light-travel delay with event ordering.

items.prompt: A star is 8 light-years from Earth. A student says a ship at 0.8c takes 10 years in Earth's frame, and since γ = 5/3 the crew ages 10 × 5/3 ≈ 16.7 years. Which diagnosis of the error is correct?

options.label: Earth's 10 years is proper time, so multiplying by γ is right, but the distance must also be contracted
The student should divide the contracted distance 4.8 ly by 0.8c, then multiply by γ, giving 10 years
The crew's clock records proper time, the shorter interval, so the correct figure is 10/γ = 6 years
Both frames measure 10 years, since γ only matters while the ship accelerates, not at steady speed

rubric: The crew's clock is present at both events, so it measures proper time, which is Earth time divided by γ.
Distractors misidentify which observer measures proper time or double-count the contraction.

items.prompt: Two events are separated by Δt = 5.0 s and Δx = 1.2e9 m in frame S (take c = 3.0e8 m/s). What time separation is measured in a frame where both events occur at the same place?
rubric: The interval is timelike: proper time = sqrt(5^2 − 4^2) = 3 s, since Δx/c = 4 s.
Distractors use Δx/c, the S time, or a simple difference of times.

items.prompt: In the twin scenario each twin sees the other's clock running slow during steady travel, yet the travelling twin ends up younger. Which analysis identifies the source of the asymmetry?

options.label: The traveller changes inertial frames at turnaround, so her simultaneity for Earth events jumps while Earth stays in one frame
Each twin's clock is slow by the same γ throughout, so the age difference comes only from signal delays
The traveller accelerates, and acceleration itself slows her clock by an extra factor that γ does not capture
Earth is at rest in an absolute sense, so dilation applies only to the traveller's clock in every analysis

rubric: Only the traveller switches inertial frames, which shifts her simultaneity assignment and breaks the symmetry.
Distractors invoke absolute rest, an extra acceleration effect on clocks, or deny a real age difference.

items.prompt: Two events are simultaneous in frame S and separated by distance Δx along x. Which statements are true when they are analysed from frames moving along x relative to S? Select all that apply.

options.label: Some inertial frame exists in which the two events occur at the same place
The spatial separation in S' is γ times the separation in S
The events are not simultaneous in S', and their order depends on the sign of the relative velocity
The spacetime interval between them is the same in both frames and is spacelike

rubric: With Δt = 0, Δt' = −γvΔx/c^2 and Δx' = γΔx, and the interval is invariant and spacelike.
No frame can make spacelike-separated events coincide in place, so the last option is false.

items.prompt: A detector bench measures an unstable particle moving at 0.8c in the lab. Its proper mean lifetime is 2.0 μs (c ≈ 3.0e8 m/s). Analysts want the mean distance it travels before decaying, as measured in the lab frame. Which value is correct?
rubric: Lab lifetime is γτ0 = 3.33 μs, so distance = 0.8c × 3.33 μs = 800 m.
480 m ignores dilation, 1333 m applies γ twice, and 288 m divides by γ.

items.prompt: A problem lists several events with coordinates in two frames and asks about a moving clock, a moving rod and the ordering of events. The criteria are to avoid misusing shortcut formulas and to keep all answers mutually consistent. Which approach is best?

options.label: Apply γ time dilation to every time difference and contraction to every length, since the shortcuts hold in any frame
Work only in the frame with the lowest speed, since the formulas are simplest there and valid for every comparison
Transform each event's (t, x) with the Lorentz equations, since shortcuts hold only for proper time or proper length
Use the Galilean transform for positions and then correct the final result with a single γ factor at the end

rubric: Dilation and contraction formulas apply only when one interval is a proper time or proper length; Lorentz transformation handles every case.
Distractors apply shortcuts universally or patch Galilean results with a single factor.

items.prompt: A claim states: a laser spot swept across the Moon's surface cannot move faster than c, because that would violate relativity. The limit applies to matter, energy and information moving between points. Which verdict is best?

options.label: Correct; the spot's speed equals the speed of the laser light, which is c in all frames of reference
Correct; any moving pattern is built from photons, so the spot's speed is capped at c in every frame
Wrong; the spot is not an object carrying information along its path, so its speed can exceed c without violating relativity
Wrong; light itself can exceed c over long distances in a vacuum, which the sweeping spot demonstrates

rubric: A sweeping spot is a sequence of separate events, not a causal signal, so no limit applies to its speed.
Distractors confuse pattern speed with signal speed or claim light can exceed c.

items.prompt: An engineer will use `½mv^2` instead of the relativistic kinetic energy provided the error stays below 1%. For small speeds the relative error is about (3/4)(v/c)^2. Which is the highest of these speeds that meets the criterion?
rubric: At 0.1c the error is about 0.75%, under 1%; at 0.3c it is about 6.8%.
0.01c also qualifies but is not the highest; larger speeds exceed the limit.

items.prompt: A student writes: 'In fission, mass is destroyed and turned into pure energy, so the total mass of the universe decreases.' Judged by conservation of energy and momentum, which critique is best?

options.label: Misleading; total energy is conserved and released energy keeps its inertia, while the products' rest masses are lower
Misleading; the products' rest masses sum to exactly the original, and E = mc^2 applies only to kinetic energy
Correct, but only for emitted photons, since released energy has no inertia and so carries no mass
Correct; E = mc^2 says mass can be turned entirely into energy, so mass is simply lost in the process

rubric: Energy carries inertia and total energy is conserved; only the rest mass of the products is lower than the original.
Distractors claim mass is destroyed, deny the mass defect, or say released energy has no inertia.

items.prompt: A student argues that a fast rod contracts because its atoms are physically squeezed by motion through a medium. Judged against the postulates of special relativity, which evaluation is best?

options.label: Rejected; contraction follows from the postulates and Lorentz transformation, with the rod's proper length unchanged
Rejected; contraction is an optical illusion from light travel times, and careful position measurements show no shortening
Accepted; the atoms are compressed by motion through the medium, which is why the shortening is measurable
Accepted in part; the rest-frame length shrinks, while moving observers see the rod keep its full length

rubric: Contraction is frame-dependent and follows from the invariance of c and the relativity of simultaneity, not from compression.
Distractors invoke an ether-like medium, call it an illusion, or reverse which observer sees contraction.

items.prompt: A student's solution to a two-frame problem is being checked. Which checks are valid tests of its correctness? Select all that apply.

options.label: The proper time of a moving clock must exceed the coordinate time between the same two events
The quantity (cΔt)^2 − (Δx)^2 matches in both frames
Each observer must find the other's rod longer than its rest length
Composite velocities of two subluminal objects stay below c
The results reduce to Galilean values when v is much smaller than c

rubric: The low-speed limit, interval invariance and the velocity bound are all genuine consistency checks.
Proper time is the shortest interval, and each observer finds the other's rod contracted, so the last two checks are wrong.

items.prompt: A mission planner must reach a star 12 light-years away in the Earth frame, ignoring acceleration. Criteria: crew proper time of at most 7 years one way, and the lowest speed from the list that meets this, to save energy. Which speed should she choose?
rubric: At 0.9c Earth time is 13.3 years and crew time is 13.3/2.294 ≈ 5.8 years, which meets the limit; 0.8c gives 9 years.
0.95c also meets the limit but is not the lowest qualifying speed.

items.prompt: A student argues that the twin paradox is self-contradictory, because each twin sees the other's clock run slow. Which critique best resolves the apparent contradiction?

options.label: Each twin's slowing cancels on reunion, so both twins are the same age and symmetry removes the apparent contradiction.
Only the traveller switches inertial frames at turnaround, which shifts her simultaneity, so the situation is asymmetric.
Time dilation affects only a twin who feels a force, so the stay-at-home twin never sees the traveller's clock run slow.
Acceleration at turnaround physically slows the traveller's clock, so a dynamical force effect, not frame switching, makes her younger.

rubric: The traveller changes inertial frames and the stay-at-home twin does not, so the two histories are not symmetric.
Distractors treat acceleration as the direct cause, deny reciprocal dilation, or assume the effects cancel.

items.prompt: Two events A and B have c^2(Δt)^2 − (Δx)^2 < 0 in one inertial frame. Which judgment about them is best supported?

options.label: Order can reverse only if a faster-than-light signal links them, so the order stays physically fixed for ordinary signals.
Some frame puts both events at the same place, because a negative interval means a slower-than-light frame exists.
Their order is the same in every frame because the interval is invariant, so A may cause B in all frames.
Some frame reverses their order, because no signal at or below c can link them, so neither event can cause the other.

rubric: Spacelike separation means no causal link, so the time order is frame-dependent.
Distractors confuse invariance of the interval with invariance of order, or mix up spacelike and timelike separation.

items.prompt: A pole of rest length 10 m moves at 0.8c through a barn of rest length 6 m. Judge the claim 'the pole fits entirely inside the barn'. Which evaluation is best?

options.label: Fitting is frame-independent, so the pole frame, where the barn is 3.6 m, shows the barn frame's claim must be an error.
Both hold: in the barn frame both doors can shut with the pole inside; in the pole frame the doors close at different times.
Only the barn frame is right, since the barn is at rest relative to the ground and so gives the true length comparison.
Contraction is only an optical appearance, so the pole never truly fits in either frame, though it seems to in one.

rubric: With γ = 5/3 the pole is 6 m in the barn frame, and 'both doors shut at once' is frame-dependent because of simultaneity.
Distractors assume a privileged frame, an invariant notion of fitting, or that contraction is merely optical.

items.prompt: You must find the threshold beam energy for p + p → p + p + p + antiproton, with the beam on a stationary proton. Which approach is best, judged on correctness and low risk of error?

options.label: Take the centre-of-mass energy as half the beam energy, since two equal-mass protons share the energy equally.
Require the beam kinetic energy to equal 2mc^2, the rest energy of the new pair, since energy conservation covers the creation.
Set the invariant E_tot^2 − (p_tot c)^2 to (4mc^2)^2, since it takes the same value in the lab and centre-of-mass frames.
Require the lab total energy to equal 4mc^2, since the four final particles must each at least have their rest energy.

rubric: At threshold all products are at rest in the CM frame, so the invariant mass must equal 4m; this accounts for momentum.
Distractors ignore the momentum the products must carry in the lab frame.

items.prompt: A writer claims: 'Push an object fast enough and its relativistic mass grows until it collapses into a black hole.' Which critique is best?

options.label: Invariant mass does not change with boosts, so a frame change cannot form a black hole; the larger energy is frame-dependent.
Contraction raises the density without limit, so it collapses for the observer who sees it moving fast, though not in its own frame.
The claim fails only because nothing massive can reach c, so the energy never becomes large enough to form a black hole.
Mass grows as γm, so beyond a critical speed the density exceeds the Schwarzschild limit and it collapses in every frame.

rubric: Whether a black hole forms is frame-independent, and the invariant mass is the same in all frames.
Distractors treat frame-dependent energy or density as physical, or argue only from the unreachability of c.

items.prompt: Which of the following judgments about special relativity are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Collinear velocities u and v always combine to u + v, with the result capped at c.
Among timelike paths joining two events, the straight inertial path records the greatest proper time.
The spacetime interval between two events has the same value in every inertial frame.
For two spacelike-separated events, some inertial frame makes them simultaneous.

rubric: The interval is invariant, spacelike events have a frame where Δt = 0, and the inertial path maximises proper time.
The velocity-addition option is false: velocities compose as (u+v)/(1+uv/c^2), not by capping a sum.

items.prompt: Cosmic-ray muons form 15 km up and travel down at 0.994c (γ ≈ 9.1). Their rest lifetime is 2.2 μs. A lab argument uses dilated lifetime (about 20 μs) against a 50 μs flight. A student says the muon-frame argument, using the 2.2 μs lifetime, must then be wrong. Which evaluation is best?

options.label: Only the lab argument is valid; the muon-frame argument fails because the muon is accelerating and so is not an inertial observer.
The muon-frame argument predicts far fewer survivors, since without dilation the muon still needs about 50 μs against a 2.2 μs lifetime.
Both arguments are valid and agree on a survival fraction near e^-2.5, since dilation in one frame matches contraction in the other.
Both effects must be applied together in one frame, dilation and contraction, otherwise the observed survival cannot be explained.

rubric: In the lab, 50 μs / 20 μs ≈ 2.5 lifetimes; in the muon frame the atmosphere is about 1.65 km, taking 5.5 μs ≈ 2.5 lifetimes.
Distractors double count the effects, dismiss the muon frame, or forget that the atmosphere contracts there.

items.prompt: An engineer needs a quantity so that successive collinear boosts combine by simple addition, and the total can never reach c. Which quantity should the design use?

options.label: Rapidity, artanh(v/c)
Momentum per unit mass, γv
Lorentz factor, γ
Speed ratio, v/c

rubric: Rapidity adds under collinear boosts, and tanh of any finite sum stays below 1.
The other quantities do not add linearly under successive boosts.

items.prompt: Design a facility to create a particle X of mass 10 GeV/c^2 in e+e- → X, with the smallest total beam energy. Which design works?

options.label: Two 10 GeV beams, e- and e+, colliding head-on
Two 5 GeV beams, e- and e+, colliding head-on
One 10 GeV electron beam on a stationary positron target
One 5 GeV electron beam on a stationary positron target

rubric: Equal head-on beams give zero total momentum, so all 10 GeV total energy becomes mass.
A fixed target gives s ≈ 2mE, far below (10 GeV)^2 for electrons.

items.prompt: A proposed test of a particle decay checks only that the total energy, including rest energy, agrees before and after in the lab frame. What must a valid test add?

options.label: A check on photon emission only, since photons are the only products whose energy and momentum are tied together.
Balance of kinetic energy alone, since rest energy is constant for each particle and so drops out of the comparison.
Total momentum balance, since a boost mixes energy and momentum, so an energy check in one frame cannot stand alone.
Separate conservation of rest mass, since the rest masses before and after the decay must match in every valid test.

rubric: Energy and momentum form a four-vector, so conservation needs both; rest mass is not conserved in general.
Distractors treat rest mass as conserved or drop momentum.

items.prompt: Ground observers must find the proper length of a rod flying past at 0.6c, which they cannot stop. Which procedure meets this?

options.label: Mark both ends at the same ground-frame instant and use the separation directly, since simultaneity removes any contraction.
Time the rod passing a fixed point and multiply by 0.6c, which gives the rest length without any further correction.
Mark both ends at the same ground-frame instant, then multiply the separation by γ = 1.25 to get the rest length.
Mark both ends at the same ground-frame instant, then divide the separation by γ = 1.25 to get the rest length.

rubric: A simultaneous ground measurement gives the contracted length L/γ, so the rest length is γ times it (10 m for 8 m).
Distractors divide instead of multiply, or treat contracted measurements as proper length.

items.prompt: A mission planner must budget the energy to speed a probe of rest mass m from 0.8c to 0.9c, in the launch frame. Which budget is correct?
rubric: Energy needed is (γ2 − γ1)mc^2 = (2.294 − 1.667)mc^2 ≈ 0.63 mc^2.
0.09 is the Newtonian ½mv^2 difference; 1.29 is the kinetic energy at 0.9c rather than the increase.

items.prompt: You design an experiment to show that a fast-moving clock runs slow because of its speed. Which features belong in a valid design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Correct for any gravitational potential difference between the moving and reference clocks.
Compare against identical lab clocks synchronised in the lab frame, using the speed measured in that frame.
Check the clocks against each other before and after the run to exclude intrinsic rate drift.
Maximise the moving clock's acceleration, since dilation is driven by acceleration rather than speed.

rubric: A valid test needs a synchronised inertial reference, drift control and control of other rate effects such as gravity.
Time dilation depends on speed, not acceleration.

items.prompt: A crew plans a cruise to a star 8 light-years away in the Sun's frame. Ignoring the acceleration phases, they want exactly 6 years to pass on board. A planner must choose the constant cruise speed that meets this requirement. Which speed works?
rubric: The proper time is 8/(βγ) = 6, so βγ = 4/3, which gives β = 0.8 with γ = 5/3.
Other speeds give about 10.7, 7.1 and 3.9 years of ship time.
